hops.afterHeading: Attention: a stronger signal, less shared noise
hops.title: Radiologists missed a gorilla in a lung scan
hops.text: Most of us assume that if our eyes land on something, we see it. In 2013, researchers asked 24 radiologists to search chest CT scans for lung nodules, the small pale spots they are trained to find. In the last case, the team had pasted in a gorilla the size of a matchbook, about 48 times the volume of an average nodule. Twenty of the 24 did not notice it. Eye-tracking showed that 12 of those 20 had looked straight at the gorilla's location, for about half a second on average. Attention set for nodules simply left the gorilla out.

sources.citation: Drew T, Võ MLH, Wolfe JM (2013). The invisible gorilla strikes again: sustained inattentional blindness in expert observers. Psychol Sci 24(9):1848-1853.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An empty chair facing a glowing greyscale scan on a monitor, with a small pale gorilla figure tucked among branching grey patterns.
image.caption: Twenty of 24 radiologists hunting for nodules missed a matchbook-sized gorilla, many while looking right at it.

hops.title: Sleepy monkeys and an ADHD medicine
hops.text: Patricia Goldman-Rakic, whose lab recorded this lesson's delay firing, and Amy Arnsten set out to test dopamine drugs on memory in aged monkeys. The compound that helped most was not a dopamine drug at all. On clonidine, as Arnsten tells it, the monkeys were almost asleep, yet performed near perfectly. Much of the benefit came from receptors on prefrontal neurons themselves. In later monkey studies, a more selective relative, guanfacine, improved memory at low doses without visible sedation, and in separate recordings, applying it near prefrontal neurons strengthened their delay firing. After clinical trials, the FDA approved an extended-release form in 2009 for ADHD in ages 6 to 17.

sources.citation: Arnsten AFT, Jin LE (2012). Guanfacine for the treatment of cognitive disorders: a century of discoveries at Yale. Yale J Biol Med 85(1):45-58.
Arnsten AFT, Cai JX, Goldman-Rakic PS (1988). The alpha-2 adrenergic agonist guanfacine improves memory in aged monkeys without sedative or hypotensive side effects. J Neurosci 8(11):4287-4298.
US FDA (2009). INTUNIV (guanfacine extended-release) prescribing information, NDA 022037.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A drowsy older macaque on a wooden perch calmly lifting one of two identical covers on a wooden tray to find a treat.
image.caption: Aged monkeys on clonidine did well on a memory task even while visibly drowsy.

hops.afterHeading: When the best correlate is not necessary
hops.title: Hunting for the Donkey Kong transistor
hops.text: In 2017, Eric Jonas and Konrad Kording turned neuroscience's tools on a system whose wiring is fully known: a simulation of the 6502 processor, whose near-twin ran the Atari 2600, playing Donkey Kong, Space Invaders and Pitfall. Recording every transistor turned up a few strongly tuned to the brightness of the last pixel drawn, like visual neurons. Then they locked each transistor on, one at a time, and checked whether each game could still draw its first frame. For 1,560 transistors, no game started; for 186, just one failed. Donkey Kong transistors? The authors call that conclusion grossly misleading: those transistors do simple general jobs, like adding binary digits.

sources.citation: Jonas E, Kording KP (2017). Could a neuroscientist understand a microprocessor? PLoS Comput Biol 13(1):e1005268.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An opened retro game console under a magnifying glass next to an old television showing blocky pixel girders and barrels.
image.caption: Lock one simulated transistor on and Donkey Kong may fail to start. That transistor still is not about Donkey Kong.

audio.title: Ants in a hurry, a sleepy monkey, and rats with rhythm
audio.transcript:
Here are three true stories where the ideas in this lesson turn up somewhere you would not expect.

The first is about acorn ants, which are small enough that a whole colony, queen and all, can live inside one hollow acorn. When a colony needs a new home, scouts lead nestmates to a candidate site one at a time. As more ants gather there, the scouts become more likely to switch to fast carrying, picking nestmates up in their jaws. The headcount at which they switch, called a quorum, works like a decision bound. In two thousand and six, Stephen Pratt and David Sumpter found that a scout was equally likely to lead or carry at about thirteen ants when the colony was leaving an intact but poor nest. When the researchers lifted the roof off a good nest to force a move, that number fell to about six. The rushed colonies moved faster, and more often split between sites or chose the worse nest. Here is the twist: the scouts also started searching and recruiting sooner, and the researchers' model suggested that mattered more than the lower headcount. Ants in a hurry turn more than one dial.

The second story starts with a surprise at Yale. Amy Arnsten and Patricia Goldman-Rakic, the same Goldman-Rakic whose lab recorded the delay firing you met in this lesson, set out to test dopamine drugs on memory in aged monkeys. The compound that helped most was not a dopamine drug at all. It was clonidine, and on it the monkeys were almost asleep and yet performed near perfectly. Doctors who already used clonidine had assumed its sedation was the source of its benefits. The monkeys suggested otherwise: much of the memory boost came from receptors on prefrontal neurons themselves. Later work showed that a more selective relative, guanfacine, improved memory in aged monkeys at low doses without visible sleepiness, and in separate recordings, applying it near prefrontal neurons strengthened their delay firing. In two thousand and nine, after clinical trials, the F D A approved an extended-release form of guanfacine as a non-stimulant treatment for A D H D in ages six to seventeen.

The third story is about rats with rhythm. In two thousand and fifteen, a team at Harvard trained rats to press a lever twice, seven hundred milliseconds apart. It took about seventeen thousand trials to get really good, and each rat settled on its own movement pattern, different from every other rat's, which it then repeated almost identically. Then the researchers destroyed motor cortex, the region long assumed to drive skilled movement, on one side of the brain. On the first day back, only one of eleven rats did worse than you would expect after an ordinary ten-day break, and it was the only rat whose routine depended on precise digit movements. Eight of the rats later lost motor cortex on the other side too, and they still performed the skill much as before. Rats that lost motor cortex on both sides before training told a different story. They were kept at it for about ninety-seven days, three times longer than normal rats need, and none of them learned the task to the standard. So these rats needed motor cortex to learn the sequence, but not to perform it once learned. The researchers suggest that motor cortex tutors older circuits below it, which can later run the skill on their own.

In the monkey study in this lesson, silencing area L I P made no measurable difference to motion discrimination in the task tested. The rats add a question about timing: a circuit can matter while an animal learns a skill that it can later perform without it.
